# Affect {#sec-affect}

[States that last]{.lb-subtitle}

<div data-life="status" data-stage="1.8"></div>

::: {.lb-takeaway}
**New:** two states that outlast what set them off: *alarm* after poison bites, *contentment* after a good meal.
They build up over several bites.

**Result:** after a run of poison bites the animals flee the bad ground; after a good meal they stay on good ground.
Both states are used in every seed.
:::

Everything this brain does so far, it does about the present. A bush is in front of it, so it bites; the skin is
cold, so it walks. When the cause is gone, the behaviour is gone in the same moment.

But some events say something about the minutes that follow. An animal that has just eaten well is probably on good
ground; one that has just been hurt is probably on bad ground. To use that, the brain has to keep something of the
event after it is over. So that the states have something to work with, the bushes in this world grow in patches
that are mostly of one kind.

<div data-life="brain" data-stage="1.8"></div>

## The circuit

Two *modulators* (substances that a few cells release and that reach many cells at once, drawn in pink) and three
new cells:

- **Alarm.** Pain releases the modulator `alarm`, which drives **`flee`**: the animal keeps going forward for a
  while, out of the poisoned ground.
- **Contentment.** **`fed`** fires when the animal tastes food and releases `serotonin`, which drives **`settle`**,
  which switches on `rest` (the cell of the previous stage that holds the forward step back). After a good meal the
  animal stays where it ate.

`hungry` still shuts `rest`. So a fed animal stays on good ground until it is hungry again, and then forages with
good bushes close by.

**The states build up.** A modulator is released in small amounts and cleared slowly, so its level is a running sum
of what happened lately. The cells that read it fire only above a threshold: one poison bite passes without alarm,
the animal flees only after more than one; it settles only after more good bites than one bush can give. One bite
says little about the ground, several bites close together say much more.

The wiring and thresholds are designed. Evolution tunes the strengths, the thresholds, and how fast each modulator
is cleared, which sets how long each state lasts.

## Watching it work

One animal from the last generation at a poison bush. It bites three times in a row, and each bite adds to `alarm`
(the row is full at the level where `flee` begins to fire). One bite is not enough. **After the third, `flee`
switches on and the animal walks away, every tick.** The alarm is cleared slowly, so the flight outlasts the pain by
more than ten ticks.

<div data-life="strip" data-stage="1.8" data-example="flight"></div>

## Biology

A drive, as in the previous stage, follows the body: the hunger cell fires as long as the stomach is empty. An
*affective state* is different in one respect: something sets it off, and then it stays for a while by itself.

In small animals such states are carried by *neuromodulators*, released quickly and cleared slowly; that slowness
is the memory. The worm *C. elegans* slows down and stays put for minutes after it has found food, under the
influence of serotonin. After a harmful touch it speeds away and keeps going well after the touch has ended.

Such a state has two sides: it is good or bad, and it makes the animal more active or less. Alarm is bad and
active; contentment is good and quiet.

## The world

The bushes now grow in patches, mostly of one kind: after good meals the neighbouring bushes are probably good,
after poison bites probably poison. Not every bush in a patch is of the patch's kind, so knowing a bush by its look,
the lesson of the association stage, still has a job.

The world is also four times larger for the same number of animals, with more food, so that animals take less food
from each other and what a better forager gains is not hidden. This is the world the next chapter starts in. The
rest is as before: cold, hot springs, and four kinds of berry bush, new in every life, half of them poison.

<div data-life="settings" data-stage="1.8"></div>

## Did it work?

<div data-life="verdict" data-stage="1.8" data-used="flee,fed,settle"></div>

**Both states are used in every seed.** `flee` costs the most when silenced: in these mixed patches a run of poison
bites is the clearest sign of bad ground.

**Against the old brain the gain is clear when the two share a world**, in every seed. Living apart, two seeds are
ahead and one is behind, so that measure alone would be inconclusive.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="All lesions, and what is not used here"}
<div data-life="lesions" data-stage="1.8"></div>

`rest`, through which both staying after a meal and staying in the warmth act, costs more than `fed` or `settle`.

Two older circuits are not used in this world:

- **`cold` and `warm_seek`.** A fed animal that walks off in search of warmth leaves the good ground; staying where
  the food is turns out to be worth more.
- **Learning.** In these patches the look of a bush and the ground it stands on say much the same thing, and the
  animals lean on the ground: two poison bites and the alarm carries them off. The learning rate is still there in
  every seed. What keeps learning from paying is that a lesson about one berry spreads to the berries that look like
  it, the problem the next chapter starts with.

Neither was removed: the next stages need the learning.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="After a bite"}
<div data-life="table" data-stage="1.8" data-example="after_a_bite"></div>

After poison bites the animals take a few more steps than the old brain, after a good meal a few fewer. The
differences are small in this measure because one bite alone no longer sets a state off.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="How a life is spent"}
<div data-life="table" data-stage="1.8" data-example="life_spent"></div>

Both populations stand still for most of their life, much of it biting at nothing: an animal held in place by
`rest` still has its grasp programme, and a bite costs little.
:::
